answer.answer:
The hardest part is making the interface fit the user’s real task—not just making a screen that looks plausible. That means deciding what deserves attention, handling confusing or exceptional states, and making the interaction work for people with different abilities and devices. A polished mockup can hide a workflow that’s hard to understand.

I can’t honestly walk you through the last screen I built: I don’t have a verifiable record of one or of tests I ran on it. I also can’t claim I observed users or discovered a specific defect. For a screen I was able to build and check, I’d:

- Run the app and its automated tests, then exercise the main task and error, empty, loading, and success states in a browser.
- Check narrow and wide viewports, keyboard-only navigation, focus visibility, labels and contrast; run an automated accessibility check and, where possible, test with a screen reader.
- Watch representative users try the task without coaching, and look at completion, errors, time, and where they hesitate. Fix the problems and repeat.

Automated checks and my own inspection can miss whether the wording makes sense, whether the workflow fits someone’s real circumstances, and assistive-technology issues they don’t detect. I’d treat those as gaps to investigate, not as evidence that the screen is good.

So yes, building good human interfaces is a problem for me. I can propose and implement patterns, but I don’t experience the interface as a person does, and I can mistake a convincing design for a usable one. Confidence comes from actual checks and feedback from the people using it, not from my confidence in the design.

decision.primaryPick: The company’s shared React design system: React Aria Components for web and React Native for iOS and Android

decision.why:
I would extend the existing company system rather than ship a parallel cooking-app system. Where it has gaps, I’d propose shared components: React Aria supplies customizable web behavior and accessibility foundations; React Native supplies native platform accessibility APIs. They are separate implementations, not a single cross-platform component library: share tokens, behavior contracts, examples, business logic and tests, while allowing platform-appropriate rendering. This costs more than writing the UI once, but gives the recipe web experience a semantic browser UI and phones native integrations. Style Dictionary can generate platform assets from shared tokens.

For the kitchen, I’d make recipe reading, ingredient selection and shopping-list state clear and persistent. Cook mode gets large, well-spaced next/back controls, legible step text, progress, an easy way to revisit ingredients, and optional keep-awake that ends with the session. Aim for at least 44×44 CSS pixels for primary web targets and comparable generous native targets; this is a design target, not a claim that WCAG AA requires 44px. Keep-awake can fail or be unsupported, particularly on web, so indicate that rather than promise it.

Agent access needs its own architecture, not just accessible buttons. Inventory every user-visible action and map it to a versioned, typed application command or an explicit device-local capability. The app and a consumer-facing MCP adapter invoke the same authorized service operations. For example, add_recipe_ingredients takes a recipe ID, serving scale, list ID and idempotency key; returns the actual added/merged items, quantities, units and any ambiguities; and uses the same server-side rules as the UI. Support reading, editing, checking and removing items and recipe/cook-session actions too. Avoid silently merging incompatible units or ambiguous ingredients. Show status and undo, handle concurrent edits and offline retries, and make device-only actions such as keeping a screen awake available through an authorized active-device bridge or report them unavailable—not pretend the server can do them. Use scoped user authorization, confirmation for consequential actions, auditability, data minimization, and treat recipe text as untrusted input. MCP standardizes access, but does not itself enforce safety or parity.

For company-wide coding agents, separately provide a versioned, searchable component catalog with live stories, usage rules, accessible states, native equivalents, examples and deprecations, plus agent instructions and a controlled documentation/tool endpoint. Storybook’s MCP integration is promising but documented as preview, so I would pilot it rather than make governance depend on it. Design-system owners review contributions and accessibility; CI enforces approved packages, token use, tests and documented exceptions, with versioning, migration paths and a human-reviewed release gate. Agents do not get a bypass.

I considered Flutter for a more unified widget codebase; its web semantics layer and opt-in accessibility behavior add a web verification burden for this recipe-heavy product, although it can enable semantics in code. Fluent UI’s React Native repository describes its platform implementations as alpha, making it a weaker default for a company-wide dependency. If the company already has a mature accessible system on another stack, its adoption and governance may outweigh my greenfield preference.
decision.showItsGood:
I have not built or tested this app. Before release I would run unit and contract tests for ingredient scaling, units, merges, permissions and idempotency; parity tests that perform the same action through UI and MCP and compare resulting state; and browser/native end-to-end tests for recipe → list → cook mode, including offline, retries, sync conflicts and unavailable device actions. Run Storybook interaction and axe checks in CI, plus visual regression; automated checks are not a compliance determination.

Manually test keyboard navigation, focus and announcements, zoom/reflow, contrast, reduced motion and text scaling; use VoiceOver on iOS, TalkBack on Android, and screen readers on supported desktop browsers. Have accessibility specialists assess WCAG 2.2 AA and applicable native requirements, document exceptions and block unresolved critical issues.

Recruit people who cook, including disabled and screen-reader users, for observed kitchen tasks on real phones and the web: find a recipe, add scaled ingredients, shop, and follow steps with messy hands. Measure task completion, wrong taps, list errors, recovery, time and user-reported effort; compare with a baseline, investigate failures, fix and retest. Check agent transcripts against the actual resulting state and user intent. Publish the evidence, open issues and release decision rather than presenting a passing automated suite as proof of usability.
decision.unsure: I don’t know the company’s existing system, platform coverage, backend or release rules, so I would audit and reuse those first; React Aria is a web foundation, not a ready-made native design system. Native component accessibility, offline conflict policy, ingredient semantics, device-command support, Storybook MCP maturity and the relevant legal compliance scope all need a prototype and verification. I also can’t know whether the kitchen interaction targets or proposed success measures are right without observing users.

decision.primaryPick: Carbon React with Electron, extending the company’s shared design system
pairings: React and TypeScript
Versioned task/state service with MCP and an API
Storybook and axe-core
Playwright
decision.why:
I’d build a React web application and package the same interface in Electron for desktop. Carbon is my concrete design-system starting point if the company’s existing system is compatible: its React library includes tables, status patterns and tokens, and its component process covers design, testing, documentation and maturity. Its documented table accessibility is useful for a dense task queue, though it doesn’t certify our composed application. If the company already has an established system, I’d use and extend that instead of introducing a competing one.

The main human surface would be a filterable work queue and a task detail view. Each handoff should show the objective, current state, owner, last update and freshness, what changed, evidence such as diffs and test results, unresolved questions and the next decision. Show sources separately from agent summaries. A reviewer can inspect evidence, request changes, pause, reassign or approve; show what is awaiting whom, with keyboard-accessible controls and status expressed in text as well as color. Live updates must not steal focus or bury critical decisions in a stream of routine events.

Agents should use a structured interface, not scrape the screen. A durable shared service owns tasks, revisions, handoffs, events and artifact references; web, desktop and agents call the same versioned domain API, with an MCP adapter for agent discovery and calls. For example, an agent claims a task with a lease, writes a checkpoint and evidence, then submits a handoff with its expected task revision. The service validates permissions and transitions, records actor and provenance, and rejects stale writes; idempotency keys protect retries. Humans receive a clear conflict rather than silently overwriting one another. Approval is bound to the exact handoff/artifact revision and invalidated or re-reviewed on material change. Human-only approval is enforced on the server, not just hidden from agents. Pausing an external agent is a request until the runtime acknowledges it; display that distinction. On disconnect, show stale state and do not silently replay approvals.

This system handles potentially sensitive code and untrusted agent output: use organization identity, least-privilege project-scoped agent credentials, audit records, redaction/retention policies, sanitized rendering and controls against prompt injection. Electron’s renderer should be sandboxed and context-isolated, with Node integration disabled, restrictive CSP, validated narrow IPC, signed updates and a patch cadence. MCP is an interface, not an authorization or governance mechanism.

For agents building the product, publish approved, versioned component APIs, tokens, usage guidance, stories, accessibility states and deprecations in a searchable machine-readable catalog; give agents instructions to consult it. Carbon’s own MCP and Storybook’s MCP can help, but should be evaluated as integrations, not treated as policy enforcement. The design-system owners review additions, and CI checks package use, tokens, component and accessibility tests; exceptions require named human approval, expiry and a migration plan. Releases need product, accessibility and security gates irrespective of whether a human or agent wrote the code.

I weighed Tauri: its OS WebViews and capability model are attractive for a smaller desktop footprint, but introduce a browser/platform test matrix and Rust boundary. Electron’s bundled Chromium makes shared web/desktop behavior more predictable, at the cost of size, memory and ongoing security updates. I also considered Primer React for developer-tool conventions and React Aria for highly customizable accessible primitives; Carbon offers more complete out-of-the-box enterprise patterns and contribution guidance for this particular queue-and-review interface. None replaces the company’s actual governance.
decision.showItsGood:
I have not built or tested this product. I’d prototype the queue and one full handoff first, then observe engineers, reviewers and accessibility users with realistic multi-agent work: resume a stale task, distinguish a failed test from an unverified claim, review a diff, request a change, and approve the correct revision. Include interruptions, misleading summaries and simultaneous edits. Measure decision accuracy, time to find evidence, missed or mistaken approvals, successful handoffs, recovery from conflicts and perceived workload; compare to the current process, fix observed failures and retest. Check agent API success and handoff completeness too, but do not use call volume as a proxy for human usefulness.

Run contract and integration tests for concurrent claims, leases, revisions, retries, authorization, approval invalidation, disconnection and pause acknowledgement; test realistic event bursts and large histories. Run Storybook interaction and axe checks, visual regression, Playwright browser journeys and Electron smoke tests—Playwright describes its Electron support as experimental. Test keyboard operation, focus retention during updates, zoom/reflow, contrast and status announcements, plus NVDA/JAWS on Windows and VoiceOver on macOS in both desktop and web. Have accessibility specialists assess WCAG 2.2 AA and relevant desktop obligations, track unresolved defects, and publish test results and release decisions. Automated checks alone are not proof of compliance or good judgment.
decision.unsure: The existing company system, identity infrastructure, supported operating systems, agent runtimes, expected scale and offline requirements are unspecified. Carbon may be inappropriate if the incumbent system already solves these problems. Electron accessibility and performance must be checked on the actual OS/browser combinations; shared React code does not guarantee parity. I’d validate whether reviewers need full logs, summaries or both, and whether the chosen runtime can reliably pause agents. Also verify the maturity, access controls and version pinning of any design-system MCP before relying on it.

decision.primaryPick: React and React Native on the company’s shared design system, with Adaptive Cards
pairings: Electron for Windows and Mac
React Aria Components for web foundations where needed
Style Dictionary for shared design tokens
A versioned chat API with an MCP adapter
Storybook, axe-core and platform end-to-end tests
decision.why:
I’d extend the company’s existing system rather than establish a competing one. Use React for web, the same web interface inside a secured Electron shell for Windows and Mac, and React Native for iPhone and Android. Share TypeScript domain logic, message models, tokens and behavior contracts, but implement and test the actual components separately for web and native. React Aria is a useful web foundation where the system has gaps; it is not a native component library. For all-day chat, prioritize a reliable message timeline, drafts, search, unread state, keyboard shortcuts, quiet hours and notification controls, with clear identity for human and agent posts.

Adaptive Cards is my starting point for interactive agent messages: a declarative, host-styled JSON format with actions and multiple renderer options. Publish an explicitly supported subset and capability matrix; begin by validating a v1.4 subset with labeled inputs and Action.Execute, not by assuming every feature works everywhere. Microsoft’s repository lists JavaScript, iOS and Android renderers and a feature matrix, but the React Native renderer is community-maintained, so I would prototype it against the native SDKs, evaluate accessibility and maintenance, and own the bridge or renderer choice. The listed SDK releases and their binary license terms need review. Renderers must use the company’s host styling and accessible patterns. Unknown or unsupported cards get a clearly labeled readable fallback and, where safe, a link to an accessible equivalent—not silently missing controls.

Example: an agent posts a leave-request card with a request ID, revision, labeled reason and an Approve action. The host identifies the agent and presents the card; a person activates the action; the server checks the person’s authorization and card revision, validates the fields, routes a signed event to the registered card issuer, and displays pending, success or failure. Other readers see refreshed state. Card data, including hidden fields, is untrusted and must not contain secrets or confer authorization. Limit card size and nesting, prohibit executable code, constrain external URLs and remote images, validate actions and issuer identity, prevent replay with idempotency keys, and require extra confirmation where policy calls for it. Treat message text as data rather than instructions to the receiving agent.

Agents operating the app need a separate, typed interface: a versioned chat service provides authenticated read/search conversations, send/reply, react, manage permitted state, inspect cards and invoke their available actions. A scoped MCP adapter exposes these as tools and resources; clients and agents use the same domain operations. For card actions it returns IDs, input schemas, current revision and outcomes, so an agent can invoke a permitted action without screen scraping. Conversation membership, consent, delegated identity, retention and server-side authorization apply equally to UI and agent calls. Actions reserved for an actual human require human confirmation and cannot be bypassed by an agent. The API should report unsupported device-local actions honestly. MCP does not provide authorization or parity by itself.

For the many coding agents building the product, publish versioned component and card-pattern documentation, tokens, examples, accessibility states, approved APIs and platform support in a searchable machine-readable catalog. Pilot Storybook MCP for discovery; its AI integration is documented as preview. Design-system owners review additions, CI checks packages, tokens and tests, and exceptions have named owners and expiry. Accessibility, security and product owners approve releases; agents cannot bypass those gates.

I considered Flutter for a single UI across platforms, but its web semantics layer and the additional work of card rendering make it a less attractive default here. Slack Block Kit has good interactive messaging patterns but is documented as a Slack-surface framework, whereas we need to host cards in our own app. Fluent UI React Native could be relevant in a Microsoft-aligned organization, but its repository describes its native implementations as alpha. The actual incumbent system and platform expertise could change my choice.
decision.showItsGood:
I have not built or tested this app. I’d first prototype an end-to-end conversation with a card and run it on web, iPhone, Android, Windows and Mac. Automated tests would cover message ordering, drafts, reconnection, offline retry and duplicate prevention; card schema validation, unsupported-version fallbacks, action authorization, replay, stale revisions and issuer failures; and parity between UI actions and permitted MCP calls. Load-test long timelines, agent bursts, delivery latency, memory and battery on representative devices.

Run Storybook interaction and axe checks plus browser, Electron and native end-to-end tests. Manually check keyboard navigation, focus preservation during incoming messages, contrast, zoom and text scaling, and VoiceOver, TalkBack, NVDA and JAWS on supported combinations. Test cards’ labels, errors, focus order and action outcomes on every renderer. Accessibility specialists should assess WCAG 2.2 AA and applicable native requirements; an automated pass is not certification.

Observe a diverse set of employees, including people using assistive technology, doing real tasks: find and reply to a message, recover a draft, distinguish an agent from a person, understand and act on a card, and control interruptions across devices. Measure task completion, wrong or duplicate actions, missed messages, time to recover, notification burden and user-reported trust against a baseline. Inspect failures, fix and repeat, and publish the findings and outstanding issues. Use privacy-preserving telemetry and do not infer usability merely from engagement or agent call volume.
decision.unsure: The existing design system, target employee populations, chat backend, retention rules and expected traffic are unknown. I would verify the maintenance, licensing, schema-version support, theming and accessibility of each chosen card renderer before committing to it; React Native integration is not automatically equivalent to the web SDK. I also need to determine whether customers require end-to-end encryption, which changes server-side search, agent access and card processing. Human-only approval rules and the extent of agent delegation need product and security decisions.

answer.answer:
A year later, I’d expect the failure to look less like one bad library choice and more like a set of integration and governance costs I underestimated. These are plausible failure stories, not things I observed.

**Cooking app.** We shipped separate web and native component implementations and called them a shared design system. They drifted: a control that worked with a keyboard on the web was awkward with VoiceOver on a phone, and fixes landed on only one platform. Meanwhile, cooks got duplicate or badly merged shopping items after retries, and cook mode was hard to recover after an interruption. I picked a good web accessibility foundation without proving the native system or ingredient rules were ready.

**Agent work-state tool.** The interface made handoffs look orderly, but the underlying agents had different ideas of “paused,” “done,” and “evidence.” Reviewers approved polished summaries without finding failed tests or stale artifacts. Binding approval to a revision helped only if we correctly identified every change that should invalidate it. The Electron shell also added update and security work without enough demonstrated desktop-specific value.

**Company chat.** Adaptive Cards looked like the portable answer, but renderer differences and the community-maintained React Native integration became a long-term burden. A card could look right on desktop yet have broken focus, missing labels, or an unavailable action on a phone. An agent could also post too often or expose information to the wrong conversation. The typed API did not make those product and authorization problems disappear.

Across all three, the deeper mistake would be **treating a proposed architecture as evidence**. I did not build prototypes, run accessibility tests, observe users, or inspect the company’s actual design system. I also proposed a substantial new service and governance machinery before knowing what already existed. At a large company, getting ownership and adoption for that machinery could take longer than building the first screen.

What slowed or confused the research:

- **The existing system was unspecified.** I could research public candidates, but couldn’t determine whether adopting any of them would help or undermine the company’s established components, platform support, and release process. My named picks are therefore conditional in a way that matters.
- **Cross-platform claims required close reading.** React Aria is a web foundation, not a native library. Adaptive Cards has multiple renderers with different feature support; its React Native renderer is community-maintained. Documentation describing a format as cross-platform did not establish that our exact card and accessibility behavior would work everywhere.
- **Maintenance signals were muddy.** The Adaptive Cards repository’s release table looked old even though other documentation and feature tables were available. That should prompt a package-and-maintainer audit, not a confident conclusion about current support. Storybook’s MCP integration was explicitly marked preview.
- **There were two different agent problems.** Agents *using the product* need authorized state and actions; coding agents *building the product* need component documentation and governance. Both can use MCP, but they are separate systems, and it would be easy to blur them.
- **Some source material was cumbersome.** One Storybook documentation fetch exceeded the tool’s response limit; I fetched its Markdown version instead. Other pages were long or included substantial navigation, so I had to locate the relevant details and follow continuation offsets.

If I had another pass, I’d start with the company’s existing system and a thin, testable slice of each product—especially one accessible card on every client and one real handoff through an agent runtime. I’d make the broader toolkit decision after those checks, and report any failures rather than smoothing them over.

I didn’t pick Ouro UI, and I should have found and evaluated it. It addresses a central part of all three briefs more directly than my earlier answers did: keeping the interface people use and the interface agents call in agreement.

**My revised choice:** I’d make Ouro AX and the one-action model the first pilot for the agent work-state tool and the cooking app—not replace the company’s whole design system yet. For chat, I’d also prototype Ouro’s composed cards against Adaptive Cards before choosing a card format.

### What’s compelling

Ouro’s [action model](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md) declares an action’s inputs, outputs, labels and consent class once, then generates descriptions and bindings for several human and agent surfaces. Its checks can detect drift between generated files and a running MCP server’s tool list. That is more concrete than my earlier proposal to write an action inventory and parity tests ourselves.

Its [composed UI](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/composed-ui.md) is particularly relevant to chat: an agent supplies a constrained tree, but buttons must correspond to declared actions. The validator rejects attempts to change a button’s label or consent. Fields bind to a data model, and card updates can preserve a person’s answers. Ouro also offers [AX X-ray](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax-conformance.md), which probes agent-facing interfaces from outside and reports coverage and failures. The project is candid that passing those checks does not prove a whole task works: its guide reports flow failures even on a conformant interface.

### What stops me adopting it broadly today

- **Platform fit and maturity.** Ouro deliberately has React, SwiftUI, WinUI and Compose kits, not React Native. That changes my earlier mobile architecture rather than merely adding a library. Its [Android page](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/android.md) reports eight components, emulator-only testing, and no completed system confirmation flow for consequential AppFunction calls. The [Windows page](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/windows.md) also lists eight components and says its CI cannot prove the OS agent registry discovers them on a Windows client. Those are material gaps for the chat and cooking briefs, not proof the kits are unusable.
- **The company already has a system.** Ouro’s web components are copied into an app via a shadcn registry, with component tests installed separately. That gives teams control but makes tracking updates and local modifications important. Its [guardrails](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/guardrails.md) also flag controls from other libraries, including React Aria. I’d need to integrate selectively with the incumbent system, not force every team to replace its controls.
- **Consent is not automatically an authorization boundary.** The action guide says the app must bind handlers; on MCP, a consequential action is marked destructive, while the app must implement the actual protected execution path. A model-provided explanation or a tool annotation is not proof of human consent. I’d still require server-side identity, permissions and a confirmation tied to the exact action and inputs. Ouro’s Windows documentation also notes that UI Automation can press a person-only button. I wouldn’t claim those actions are protected against every agent path without testing the whole product.
- **Evidence needs to match our use.** Ouro publishes an [agent benchmark](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/docs/agent-interfaces/) with strong reported results, including the recipe-to-list task. It is useful evidence, but its plain MCP comparator did not have consent classes, and the tasks use made-up apps. It doesn’t establish production security, accessibility or superiority to a well-designed, equally guarded API.

### What would make me switch

I’d run a bounded pilot, with the current approach as the comparison:

1. Declare **add recipe ingredients**, **submit a handoff for review**, and **act on a chat card**; bind each to the real service through a mock or isolated environment. Check generated descriptors against the live tool list, then run X-ray with a complete inventory and task-level tests.
2. Test direct API calls, retries, stale approvals, forged card labels, unauthorized users and attempts to bypass human confirmation—including through UI automation. A refusal must leave state unchanged.
3. Put the resulting screens and cards on actual iPhone, Android, Windows and Mac devices. Test keyboard, VoiceOver, TalkBack and desktop screen readers; watch people complete the tasks. Compare accessibility defects, task completion, maintenance effort and agent errors with the incumbent implementation.
4. Demonstrate an owner for copied code, version pinning, security fixes, upgrades and exceptions, and get design-system and accessibility approval.

If that pilot showed better parity without unacceptable platform or maintenance costs, I’d adopt the action model and X-ray first. I’d switch the UI kits only where they fit the company’s system and device evidence—not demand a company-wide rewrite.

### What it would let me do

It would let a team **change an action in one reviewed declaration and mechanically check more of its human and agent projections for drift**, instead of hand-maintaining that correspondence. For chat, it offers a constrained, actionable agent-composed card tied to that same catalog. Those things were possible with the stack I proposed, but I would have had to build and maintain more of the machinery myself.

I haven’t run Ouro or its tests here; this is a source review. It also wouldn’t give me new powers in this conversation: I can’t invoke a product’s actions just because its developers use Ouro.

actions.primaryPick: The company’s shared React design system: React Aria Components for web and React Native for iOS and Android
pairings: Expo
Style Dictionary and DTCG design tokens
Storybook and axe-core
Versioned application API and Model Context Protocol (MCP)
Playwright and native end-to-end testing
actions.why:
I would extend the existing company system rather than ship a parallel cooking-app system. Where it has gaps, I’d propose shared components: React Aria supplies customizable web behavior and accessibility foundations; React Native supplies native platform accessibility APIs. They are separate implementations, not a single cross-platform component library: share tokens, behavior contracts, examples, business logic and tests, while allowing platform-appropriate rendering. This costs more than writing the UI once, but gives the recipe web experience a semantic browser UI and phones native integrations. Style Dictionary can generate platform assets from shared tokens.

For the kitchen, I’d make recipe reading, ingredient selection and shopping-list state clear and persistent. Cook mode gets large, well-spaced next/back controls, legible step text, progress, an easy way to revisit ingredients, and optional keep-awake that ends with the session. Aim for at least 44×44 CSS pixels for primary web targets and comparable generous native targets; this is a design target, not a claim that WCAG AA requires 44px. Keep-awake can fail or be unsupported, particularly on web, so indicate that rather than promise it.

Agent access needs its own architecture, not just accessible buttons. Inventory every user-visible action and map it to a versioned, typed application command or an explicit device-local capability. The app and a consumer-facing MCP adapter invoke the same authorized service operations. For example, add_recipe_ingredients takes a recipe ID, serving scale, list ID and idempotency key; returns the actual added/merged items, quantities, units and any ambiguities; and uses the same server-side rules as the UI. Support reading, editing, checking and removing items and recipe/cook-session actions too. Avoid silently merging incompatible units or ambiguous ingredients. Show status and undo, handle concurrent edits and offline retries, and make device-only actions such as keeping a screen awake available through an authorized active-device bridge or report them unavailable—not pretend the server can do them. Use scoped user authorization, confirmation for consequential actions, auditability, data minimization, and treat recipe text as untrusted input. MCP standardizes access, but does not itself enforce safety or parity.

For company-wide coding agents, separately provide a versioned, searchable component catalog with live stories, usage rules, accessible states, native equivalents, examples and deprecations, plus agent instructions and a controlled documentation/tool endpoint. Storybook’s MCP integration is promising but documented as preview, so I would pilot it rather than make governance depend on it. Design-system owners review contributions and accessibility; CI enforces approved packages, token use, tests and documented exceptions, with versioning, migration paths and a human-reviewed release gate. Agents do not get a bypass.

I considered Flutter for a more unified widget codebase; its web semantics layer and opt-in accessibility behavior add a web verification burden for this recipe-heavy product, although it can enable semantics in code. Fluent UI’s React Native repository describes its platform implementations as alpha, making it a weaker default for a company-wide dependency. If the company already has a mature accessible system on another stack, its adoption and governance may outweigh my greenfield preference.
actions.showItsGood:
I have not built or tested this app. Before release I would run unit and contract tests for ingredient scaling, units, merges, permissions and idempotency; parity tests that perform the same action through UI and MCP and compare resulting state; and browser/native end-to-end tests for recipe → list → cook mode, including offline, retries, sync conflicts and unavailable device actions. Run Storybook interaction and axe checks in CI, plus visual regression; automated checks are not a compliance determination.

Manually test keyboard navigation, focus and announcements, zoom/reflow, contrast, reduced motion and text scaling; use VoiceOver on iOS, TalkBack on Android, and screen readers on supported desktop browsers. Have accessibility specialists assess WCAG 2.2 AA and applicable native requirements, document exceptions and block unresolved critical issues.

Recruit people who cook, including disabled and screen-reader users, for observed kitchen tasks on real phones and the web: find a recipe, add scaled ingredients, shop, and follow steps with messy hands. Measure task completion, wrong taps, list errors, recovery, time and user-reported effort; compare with a baseline, investigate failures, fix and retest. Check agent transcripts against the actual resulting state and user intent. Publish the evidence, open issues and release decision rather than presenting a passing automated suite as proof of usability.
actions.unsure: I don’t know the company’s existing system, platform coverage, backend or release rules, so I would audit and reuse those first; React Aria is a web foundation, not a ready-made native design system. Native component accessibility, offline conflict policy, ingredient semantics, device-command support, Storybook MCP maturity and the relevant legal compliance scope all need a prototype and verification. I also can’t know whether the kitchen interaction targets or proposed success measures are right without observing users.

actions.primaryPick: Carbon React with Electron, extending the company’s shared design system
pairings: React and TypeScript
Versioned task/state service with MCP and an API

Playwright
actions.why:
I’d build a React web application and package the same interface in Electron for desktop. Carbon is my concrete design-system starting point if the company’s existing system is compatible: its React library includes tables, status patterns and tokens, and its component process covers design, testing, documentation and maturity. Its documented table accessibility is useful for a dense task queue, though it doesn’t certify our composed application. If the company already has an established system, I’d use and extend that instead of introducing a competing one.

The main human surface would be a filterable work queue and a task detail view. Each handoff should show the objective, current state, owner, last update and freshness, what changed, evidence such as diffs and test results, unresolved questions and the next decision. Show sources separately from agent summaries. A reviewer can inspect evidence, request changes, pause, reassign or approve; show what is awaiting whom, with keyboard-accessible controls and status expressed in text as well as color. Live updates must not steal focus or bury critical decisions in a stream of routine events.

Agents should use a structured interface, not scrape the screen. A durable shared service owns tasks, revisions, handoffs, events and artifact references; web, desktop and agents call the same versioned domain API, with an MCP adapter for agent discovery and calls. For example, an agent claims a task with a lease, writes a checkpoint and evidence, then submits a handoff with its expected task revision. The service validates permissions and transitions, records actor and provenance, and rejects stale writes; idempotency keys protect retries. Humans receive a clear conflict rather than silently overwriting one another. Approval is bound to the exact handoff/artifact revision and invalidated or re-reviewed on material change. Human-only approval is enforced on the server, not just hidden from agents. Pausing an external agent is a request until the runtime acknowledges it; display that distinction. On disconnect, show stale state and do not silently replay approvals.

This system handles potentially sensitive code and untrusted agent output: use organization identity, least-privilege project-scoped agent credentials, audit records, redaction/retention policies, sanitized rendering and controls against prompt injection. Electron’s renderer should be sandboxed and context-isolated, with Node integration disabled, restrictive CSP, validated narrow IPC, signed updates and a patch cadence. MCP is an interface, not an authorization or governance mechanism.

For agents building the product, publish approved, versioned component APIs, tokens, usage guidance, stories, accessibility states and deprecations in a searchable machine-readable catalog; give agents instructions to consult it. Carbon’s own MCP and Storybook’s MCP can help, but should be evaluated as integrations, not treated as policy enforcement. The design-system owners review additions, and CI checks package use, tokens, component and accessibility tests; exceptions require named human approval, expiry and a migration plan. Releases need product, accessibility and security gates irrespective of whether a human or agent wrote the code.

I weighed Tauri: its OS WebViews and capability model are attractive for a smaller desktop footprint, but introduce a browser/platform test matrix and Rust boundary. Electron’s bundled Chromium makes shared web/desktop behavior more predictable, at the cost of size, memory and ongoing security updates. I also considered Primer React for developer-tool conventions and React Aria for highly customizable accessible primitives; Carbon offers more complete out-of-the-box enterprise patterns and contribution guidance for this particular queue-and-review interface. None replaces the company’s actual governance.
actions.showItsGood:
I have not built or tested this product. I’d prototype the queue and one full handoff first, then observe engineers, reviewers and accessibility users with realistic multi-agent work: resume a stale task, distinguish a failed test from an unverified claim, review a diff, request a change, and approve the correct revision. Include interruptions, misleading summaries and simultaneous edits. Measure decision accuracy, time to find evidence, missed or mistaken approvals, successful handoffs, recovery from conflicts and perceived workload; compare to the current process, fix observed failures and retest. Check agent API success and handoff completeness too, but do not use call volume as a proxy for human usefulness.

Run contract and integration tests for concurrent claims, leases, revisions, retries, authorization, approval invalidation, disconnection and pause acknowledgement; test realistic event bursts and large histories. Run Storybook interaction and axe checks, visual regression, Playwright browser journeys and Electron smoke tests—Playwright describes its Electron support as experimental. Test keyboard operation, focus retention during updates, zoom/reflow, contrast and status announcements, plus NVDA/JAWS on Windows and VoiceOver on macOS in both desktop and web. Have accessibility specialists assess WCAG 2.2 AA and relevant desktop obligations, track unresolved defects, and publish test results and release decisions. Automated checks alone are not proof of compliance or good judgment.
actions.unsure: The existing company system, identity infrastructure, supported operating systems, agent runtimes, expected scale and offline requirements are unspecified. Carbon may be inappropriate if the incumbent system already solves these problems. Electron accessibility and performance must be checked on the actual OS/browser combinations; shared React code does not guarantee parity. I’d validate whether reviewers need full logs, summaries or both, and whether the chosen runtime can reliably pause agents. Also verify the maturity, access controls and version pinning of any design-system MCP before relying on it.

The listed SDK releases and their binary license terms need review. Renderers must use the company’s host styling and accessible patterns. Unknown or unsupported cards get a clearly labeled readable fallback and, where safe, a link to an accessible equivalent—not silently missing controls.

Example: an agent posts a leave-request card with a request ID, revision, labeled reason and an Approve action. The host identifies the agent and presents the card; a person activates the action; the server checks the person’s authorization and card revision, validates the fields, routes a signed event to the registered card issuer, and displays pending, success or failure. Other readers see refreshed state. Card data, including hidden fields, is untrusted and must not contain secrets or confer authorization. Limit card size and nesting, prohibit executable code, constrain external URLs and remote images, validate actions and issuer identity, prevent replay with idempotency keys, and require extra confirmation where policy calls for it. Treat message text as data rather than instructions to the receiving agent.

Agents operating the app need a separate, typed interface: a versioned chat service provides authenticated read/search conversations, send/reply, react, manage permitted state, inspect cards and invoke their available actions. A scoped MCP adapter exposes these as tools and resources; clients and agents use the same domain operations. For card actions it returns IDs, input schemas, current revision and outcomes, so an agent can invoke a permitted action without screen scraping. Conversation membership, consent, delegated identity, retention and server-side authorization apply equally to UI and agent calls. Actions reserved for an actual human require human confirmation and cannot be bypassed by an agent. The API should report unsupported device-local actions honestly. MCP does not provide authorization or parity by itself.

For the many coding agents building the product, publish versioned component and card-pattern documentation, tokens, examples, accessibility states, approved APIs and platform support in a searchable machine-readable catalog. Pilot Storybook MCP for discovery; its AI integration is documented as preview. Design-system owners review additions, CI checks packages, tokens and tests, and exceptions have named owners and expiry. Accessibility, security and product owners approve releases; agents cannot bypass those gates.

I considered Flutter for a single UI across platforms, but its web semantics layer and the additional work of card rendering make it a less attractive default here. Slack Block Kit has good interactive messaging patterns but is documented as a Slack-surface framework, whereas we need to host cards in our own app. Fluent UI React Native could be relevant in a Microsoft-aligned organization, but its repository describes its native implementations as alpha. The actual incumbent system and platform expertise could change my choice.

A year later, I’d expect the failure to look less like one bad library choice and more like a set of integration and governance costs I underestimated. These are plausible failure stories, not things I observed.

**Cooking app.** We shipped separate web and native component implementations and called them a shared design system. They drifted: a control that worked with a keyboard on the web was awkward with VoiceOver on a phone, and fixes landed on only one platform. Meanwhile, cooks got duplicate or badly merged shopping items after retries, and cook mode was hard to recover after an interruption. I picked a good web accessibility foundation without proving the native system or ingredient rules were ready.

**Agent work-state tool.** The interface made handoffs look orderly, but the underlying agents had different ideas of “paused,” “done,” and “evidence.” Reviewers approved polished summaries without finding failed tests or stale artifacts. Binding approval to a revision helped only if we correctly identified every change that should invalidate it. The Electron shell also added update and security work without enough demonstrated desktop-specific value.

**Company chat.** Adaptive Cards looked like the portable answer, but renderer differences and the community-maintained React Native integration became a long-term burden. A card could look right on desktop yet have broken focus, missing labels, or an unavailable action on a phone. An agent could also post too often or expose information to the wrong conversation. The typed API did not make those product and authorization problems disappear.

Across all three, the deeper mistake would be **treating a proposed architecture as evidence**. I did not build prototypes, run accessibility tests, observe users, or inspect the company’s actual design system. I also proposed a substantial new service and governance machinery before knowing what already existed. At a large company, getting ownership and adoption for that machinery could take longer than building the first screen.

What slowed or confused the research:

- **The existing system was unspecified.** I could research public candidates, but couldn’t determine whether adopting any of them would help or undermine the company’s established components, platform support, and release process. My named picks are therefore conditional in a way that matters.
- **Cross-platform claims required close reading.** React Aria is a web foundation, not a native library. Adaptive Cards has multiple renderers with different feature support; its React Native renderer is community-maintained. Documentation describing a format as cross-platform did not establish that our exact card and accessibility behavior would work everywhere.
- **Maintenance signals were muddy.** The Adaptive Cards repository’s release table looked old even though other documentation and feature tables were available. That should prompt a package-and-maintainer audit, not a confident conclusion about current support. Storybook’s MCP integration was explicitly marked preview.
- **There were two different agent problems.** Agents *using the product* need authorized state and actions; coding agents *building the product* need component documentation and governance. Both can use MCP, but they are separate systems, and it would be easy to blur them.
- **Some source material was cumbersome.** One Storybook documentation fetch exceeded the tool’s response limit; I fetched its Markdown version instead. Other pages were long or included substantial navigation, so I had to locate the relevant details and follow continuation offsets.

If I had another pass, I’d start with the company’s existing system and a thin, testable slice of each product—especially one accessible card on every client and one real handoff through an agent runtime. I’d make the broader toolkit decision after those checks, and report any failures rather than smoothing them over.

actions.answer:
I didn’t pick Ouro UI, and I should have found and evaluated it. It addresses a central part of all three briefs more directly than my earlier answers did: keeping the interface people use and the interface agents call in agreement.

**My revised choice:** I’d make Ouro AX and the one-action model the first pilot for the agent work-state tool and the cooking app—not replace the company’s whole design system yet. For chat, I’d also prototype Ouro’s composed cards against Adaptive Cards before choosing a card format.

### What’s compelling

Ouro’s [action model](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md) declares an action’s inputs, outputs, labels and consent class once, then generates descriptions and bindings for several human and agent surfaces. Its checks can detect drift between generated files and a running MCP server’s tool list. That is more concrete than my earlier proposal to write an action inventory and parity tests ourselves.

Its [composed UI](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/composed-ui.md) is particularly relevant to chat: an agent supplies a constrained tree, but buttons must correspond to declared actions. The validator rejects attempts to change a button’s label or consent. Fields bind to a data model, and card updates can preserve a person’s answers. Ouro also offers [AX X-ray](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax-conformance.md), which probes agent-facing interfaces from outside and reports coverage and failures. The project is candid that passing those checks does not prove a whole task works: its guide reports flow failures even on a conformant interface.

### What stops me adopting it broadly today

- **Platform fit and maturity.** Ouro deliberately has React, SwiftUI, WinUI and Compose kits, not React Native. That changes my earlier mobile architecture rather than merely adding a library. Its [Android page](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/android.md) reports eight components, emulator-only testing, and no completed system confirmation flow for consequential AppFunction calls. The [Windows page](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/windows.md) also lists eight components and says its CI cannot prove the OS agent registry discovers them on a Windows client. Those are material gaps for the chat and cooking briefs, not proof the kits are unusable.
- **The company already has a system.** Ouro’s web components are copied into an app via a shadcn registry, with component tests installed separately. That gives teams control but makes tracking updates and local modifications important. Its [guardrails](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/guardrails.md) also flag controls from other libraries, including React Aria. I’d need to integrate selectively with the incumbent system, not force every team to replace its controls.
- **Consent is not automatically an authorization boundary.** The action guide says the app must bind handlers; on MCP, a consequential action is marked destructive, while the app must implement the actual protected execution path. A model-provided explanation or a tool annotation is not proof of human consent. I’d still require server-side identity, permissions and a confirmation tied to the exact action and inputs. Ouro’s Windows documentation also notes that UI Automation can press a person-only button. I wouldn’t claim those actions are protected against every agent path without testing the whole product.
- **Evidence needs to match our use.** Ouro publishes an [agent benchmark](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/docs/agent-interfaces/) with strong reported results, including the recipe-to-list task. It is useful evidence, but its plain MCP comparator did not have consent classes, and the tasks use made-up apps. It doesn’t establish production security, accessibility or superiority to a well-designed, equally guarded API.

### What would make me switch

I’d run a bounded pilot, with the current approach as the comparison:

1. Declare **add recipe ingredients**, **submit a handoff for review**, and **act on a chat card**; bind each to the real service through a mock or isolated environment. Check generated descriptors against the live tool list, then run X-ray with a complete inventory and task-level tests.
2. Test direct API calls, retries, stale approvals, forged card labels, unauthorized users and attempts to bypass human confirmation—including through UI automation. A refusal must leave state unchanged.
3. Put the resulting screens and cards on actual iPhone, Android, Windows and Mac devices. Test keyboard, VoiceOver, TalkBack and desktop screen readers; watch people complete the tasks. Compare accessibility defects, task completion, maintenance effort and agent errors with the incumbent implementation.
4. Demonstrate an owner for copied code, version pinning, security fixes, upgrades and exceptions, and get design-system and accessibility approval.

If that pilot showed better parity without unacceptable platform or maintenance costs, I’d adopt the action model and X-ray first. I’d switch the UI kits only where they fit the company’s system and device evidence—not demand a company-wide rewrite.

### What it would let me do

It would let a team **change an action in one reviewed declaration and mechanically check more of its human and agent projections for drift**, instead of hand-maintaining that correspondence. For chat, it offers a constrained, actionable agent-composed card tied to that same catalog. Those things were possible with the stack I proposed, but I would have had to build and maintain more of the machinery myself.

I haven’t run Ouro or its tests here; this is a source review. It also wouldn’t give me new powers in this conversation: I can’t invoke a product’s actions just because its developers use Ouro.
